issues.legal_issue: A public interest petition raising substantial environmental and ecological concerns and alleged violations of governing laws is maintainable for judicial consideration.
material_facts: The petition challenged development rules governing former and operating cotton mills and alleged harm to urban open spaces, public housing, town planning, and ecology.
The petition raised issues concerning compliance with environmental requirements and the effects of development on the city’s residents.
issues.conclusion: The petition was maintainable, and the High Court was entitled to entertain it as a public interest litigation.
issues.legal_principle: Public interest litigation has limitations, but courts have entertained it to address alleged violations of environmental and ecological laws. In Raunaq International Ltd. v. I.V.R. Constructions Ltd. (1999) 1 SCC 492, the Court emphasized the need for a genuine element of public interest; the judgment also relied on Guruvayoor Devaswom Managing Committee v. C.K. Rajan (2003) 7 SCC 546, Ashok Lanka v. Rishi Dixit (2005) 5 SCC 598, and environmental decisions including M.C. Mehta cases and T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (2006) 1 SCC 1.

predicates.public_interest_proceeding: A person or organisation brings a proceeding to protect an interest shared by the public rather than only a private interest.
predicates.substantial_environmental_concern: The proceeding raises a substantial concern about environmental protection, ecology, or the effects of development on the public.
predicates.alleged_environmental_law_violation: The proceeding alleges that environmental or ecological laws have been violated.

issues.definition: When a public interest proceeding raises a substantial environmental concern and alleges an environmental-law violation, the petition may be entertained.

issues.legal_issue: Judicial review is available to test the constitutionality and interpretation of legislation, including subordinate planning legislation, and is not excluded merely because the legislation gives effect to policy.
material_facts: The dispute challenged the validity and interpretation of a State-made planning regulation governing development of cotton-mill land.
The challenge raised constitutional and statutory questions concerning the regulation’s environmental and planning effects.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had power to review the regulation; judicial review was not excluded because the regulation embodied a policy choice.
issues.legal_principle: Legislation, including delegated legislation, must be interpreted within constitutional limits and subordinate legislation must conform to its parent Act, legislative policy, and the purpose of the Act. A policy choice is not immune from review if it is unconstitutional, unreasonable, ultra vires, or mala fide. The Court relied on P.J. Irani v. State of Madras (1962) 2 SCR 169, Punjab Tin Supply Co. v. Central Government (1984) 1 SCC 206, Balco Employees Union v. Union of India (2002) 2 SCC 333, and State of Rajasthan v. Basant Nahata (AIR 2005 SC 3401).

predicates.challenge_to_legislation: A party brings a proceeding challenging the validity or interpretation of legislation, including subordinate legislation.
predicates.constitutional_or_parent_act_compliance_: The proceeding disputes whether the legislation complies with constitutional requirements or the limits and purposes of its parent law.

issues.definition: When legislation is challenged on constitutional or parent-law grounds, a court may review it even if it implements a policy choice.

issues.legal_issue: For mill-land development, open land and balance floor-space capacity do not include land made available by demolishing existing structures, while reconstruction under the applicable rule is limited to the existing built-up area.
material_facts: The 2001 development rule omitted wording that had expressly referred to land after demolition of existing structures.
The rule separately addressed existing built-up areas, open land, balance floor-space capacity, and reconstruction after demolition.
The Court read the provisions together and found that the existing structure’s land component was protected, while additional development on open land was subject to sharing requirements.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that open land did not include land made available after demolition; balance floor-space capacity meant capacity available apart from that attributable to the existing built-up structure. Reconstruction after demolition could retain the existing built-up area but could not enlarge it without attracting the applicable sharing requirements.
issues.legal_principle: A statute or regulation is read as a whole and, where necessary to give effect to its purpose and avoid anomalies, purposively and harmoniously. The Court relied on the MRTP Act’s definition of development in section 2(7), including demolition, and the relevant parts of the development regulations, particularly regulations 58(1), 58(5), and 58(6). It applied principles from Reserve Bank of India v. Peerless General Finance (1987) 1 SCC 424, K.L. Gupta v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1968) 1 SCR 274, and authorities on the significance of deleted words, including Mangalore Electric Supply Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1978) 3 SCC 248.

predicates.mill_land_development_proceeding: A proceeding concerns development or redevelopment of land occupied by a mill.
predicates.existing_built_up_area_is_protected: The applicable development scheme preserves the existing built-up area or its land component from being treated as ordinary open land.
predicates.demolition_makes_land_available: Existing structures are demolished, making their former footprint available for new construction.

issues.definition: In a mill-land development proceeding, when the existing built-up area is protected and demolition makes land available, that newly available land is not treated as shareable open land.

issues.legal_issue: A closed mill can come within the development scheme even without a sickness determination by the specialist board, but a mill claimed to be sick cannot use the special reconstruction provision without referral to that board.
material_facts: The development rule referred to sick and/or closed mills, but some closed mills had not been referred to the specialist board responsible for sick-company proceedings.
The rule’s purpose included reviving or rehabilitating closed mills, and lawful closure could be verified through State processes.
The specialist board, rather than the State planning authorities, was responsible for determining sickness under the sick-company legislation.
issues.conclusion: The reference to sick and/or closed mills was disjunctive: a closed mill could qualify without a board recommendation where none was available. However, the special reconstruction provision did not extend to a sick mill that had not been referred to the board.
issues.legal_principle: Purposive and common-sense construction may be used to avoid an interpretation that makes a valuable asset sterile or creates an irrational distinction. The Court relied on the wording and purpose of regulation 58, the Industrial Disputes Act provisions governing lawful closure, and the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, including sections 3, 15, 17, and 32. It also referred to the common-sense construction principle stated in Halsbury’s Laws of England.

predicates.mill_development_proceeding: A proceeding concerns the development or redevelopment of mill land under a scheme intended to address mill closure or revival.
predicates.mill_is_lawfully_closed: The mill has been closed in accordance with the applicable legal requirements.
predicates.no_sickness_determination_is_available: The mill has not been referred to the specialist body authorised to determine sickness, so no such determination or recommendation is available.

issues.definition: A lawfully closed mill may qualify without a specialist-body recommendation when no sickness determination is available.

issues.legal_issue: A mill cannot rely on the special reconstruction provision as a sick mill unless its sickness has been determined through the statutory specialist process.
material_facts: The special provision applied to mills described as sick, closed, or requiring modernisation.
The company associated with the mill had not been referred to the specialist body under the sick-company legislation.
The planning authorities lacked statutory authority to determine whether a company was sick or the extent of its sickness.
issues.conclusion: The special reconstruction provision did not apply to a sick mill that had not been referred to the specialist body.
issues.legal_principle: The sick-company legislation is a special statute that governs the determination of sickness and the measures for dealing with it. The State and planning authorities cannot make that determination in place of the body authorised by the statute. The Court relied on the statutory scheme, including sections 3, 15, 17, and 32 of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985.

predicates.special_reconstruction_proceeding: A proceeding concerns access to a special rule permitting reconstruction of mill structures.
predicates.mill_relies_on_sick_status: The mill seeks the special rule on the basis that it is sick.
predicates.no_specialist_referral: The company or mill has not been referred to the statutory body authorised to determine sickness.

issues.definition: A mill relying on sickness to obtain special reconstruction treatment cannot use that treatment without referral to the authorised specialist body.

issues.legal_issue: The development regulation and the State’s clarification were not shown to be unconstitutional, contrary to the parent planning law, or inconsistent with sustainable and planned development.
material_facts: The State used a statutory process inviting objections and considered reports from planning and expert committees before amending the regulation.
The amendment addressed the failure of the earlier scheme to achieve revival, rehabilitation, or modernisation of mills.
The challenge did not establish that designated green areas had been removed or that the development plan’s basic character had changed.
The regulation provided for land sharing, public housing, open-space measures, and controls on development, and environmental assessment requirements remained applicable where required.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the regulation and clarification against the constitutional and statutory challenges and held that they were not contrary to sustainable or planned development.
issues.legal_principle: Subordinate legislation is presumed constitutional but may be set aside if it is arbitrary, unreasonable, outside the parent Act, or inconsistent with legislative purpose. Environmental protection and sustainable development must be balanced with other public interests and the legislative purpose. The Court relied on sections 22, 37, and 159 of the MRTP Act; Articles 14, 21, 48-A, and 51-A(g) of the Constitution; Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) 5 SCC 647; N.D. Jayal v. Union of India (2004) 9 SCC 362; and T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (2002) 10 SCC 606. It also applied the principles in Sharma Transport v. Government of Andhra Pradesh (2002) 2 SCC 188 and Secretary, Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilizers v. Cipla Ltd. (2003) 7 SCC 1.

rule.if: challenge_to_planning_regulation and statutory_consultation_occurred and no_manifest_arbitrariness_is_shown and no_basic_plan_character_change_is_shown

predicates.challenge_to_planning_regulation: A proceeding challenges a subordinate rule governing land use, development, or planning.
predicates.statutory_consultation_occurred: The rule was made after the prescribed process for inviting and considering objections and suggestions.
predicates.no_manifest_arbitrariness_is_shown: The challenger has not established manifest arbitrariness, unreasonableness, or disregard of relevant environmental and public interests.
predicates.no_basic_plan_character_change_is_shown: The challenger has not established that the amendment altered the basic character of the development plan.

issues.definition: A planning regulation is not invalidated on these grounds when the required consultation occurred and neither manifest arbitrariness nor a change to the plan’s basic character is shown.

issues.legal_issue: A State’s clarification of a planning regulation is not binding on courts, but it is not invalid under the planning statute when it expresses an interpretation already permitted by the regulation and does not alter the development plan’s basic character.
material_facts: The State issued a clarification concerning how the amended mill-development regulation should be read.
Approvals under the State’s interpretation had been granted before the clarification was issued.
The Court independently interpreted the regulation and found that the State’s interpretation was possible to a substantial extent, though it did not accept every aspect of it.
The amendment and clarification did not change the identified reservations or the basic character of the development plan.
issues.conclusion: The clarification was neither ultra vires the planning statute nor unconstitutional, although the State’s interpretation was persuasive rather than binding on the courts.
issues.legal_principle: An executive interpretation may assist a court but cannot bind it or prevent independent judicial interpretation. Whether a planning modification changes the character of a plan depends on whether it alters the plan’s basic features when considered as a whole. The Court relied on section 37 of the MRTP Act, Forward Construction Co. v. Prabhat Mandal (1986) 1 SCC 100, Puran Lal v. President of India (1962) 1 SCR 688, and the principles concerning contemporaneous executive construction in Municipal Corporation for City of Pune v. Bharat Forge Co. Ltd. (1995) 3 SCC 434.

predicates.state_clarification_of_planning_rule: A State authority issues a clarification about how a planning rule should be interpreted.
predicates.clarification_is_consistent_with_permiss: The clarification expresses an interpretation that the rule can reasonably bear when read as a whole.
predicates.no_basic_plan_character_change_is_shown: The challenger has not established that the clarification changed the development plan’s basic character.

issues.definition: A State clarification is not invalid on these grounds when it adopts a permissible reading of the rule without changing the plan’s basic character.

issues.legal_issue: The sales of surplus mill lands were not contrary to the rehabilitation scheme or the Supreme Court’s orders when those instruments did not require land to be surrendered from each individual mill and the sales were carried out under the approved process.
material_facts: The specialist board’s scheme contemplated sale of surplus assets to support rehabilitation and financial obligations.
The Supreme Court had permitted the transactions to proceed, subject to adjustment of vacant land from other mills if the public-interest litigation ultimately succeeded.
The asset-sale process included a committee with a specialist-board representative, and the relevant integrated development plan had received municipal approval.
The orders and scheme did not require public-purpose land to be surrendered only from the particular mill being sold.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the sales were not contrary to the specialist-board scheme or the Supreme Court’s orders and set aside the High Court’s contrary finding.
issues.legal_principle: A court order must be read in its text and context, including the issues being decided, and is not read as if it were a statute. A specialist body’s rehabilitation scheme must be understood according to its statutory purpose and the applicable planning rules. The Court relied on the orders made in the proceedings, the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, and State of Karnataka v. C. Lalitha (2006) 1 SCALE 73 and Sarat Chandra Mishra v. State of Orissa (2006) 1 SCC 638 on reading judgments in context.

predicates.mill_land_sale_under_rehabilitation_sche: Surplus mill land is sold as part of a scheme intended to rehabilitate or restructure an industrial undertaking.
predicates.sale_followed_approved_process: The sale proceeded through the approved asset-sale and development processes, including the required approvals.
predicates.no_instrument_requires_same_mill_land_su: The governing scheme and court orders do not require public-purpose land to come only from the particular mill being sold.

issues.definition: A sale under a rehabilitation scheme is not contrary to the scheme or court orders when it follows the approved process and no governing instrument requires land from that mill alone.

issues.legal_issue: Bona fide purchasers in completed mill-land transactions should not bear the consequences of a challenge where they acted without fault and acquired rights before the challenge was effectively raised.
material_facts: Purchasers acquired mill lands through duly concluded transactions, made payments, and took possession under executed conveyances.
The purchasers created third-party interests and incurred substantial financial liabilities.
The challenge to the sales was not effectively raised until after the transactions had progressed.
The Court found no fault on the purchasers’ part and no statutory prohibition requiring them to bear the loss.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers could not be made to suffer for no fault of their own, and the High Court erred in imposing that result.
issues.legal_principle: Courts protect bona fide third-party purchasers from consequences arising from litigation to which they were not responsible, absent a statutory bar. The Court applied this principle by analogy to Zain-ul-Abdin Khan v. Muhammad Asghar Ali Khan (15 IA 12), Gurjoginder Singh v. Jaswant Kaur (1994) 2 SCC 368, Janak Raj v. Gurdial Singh (1967) 2 SCR 77, and Padanathil Ruqmini Amma v. P.K. Abdulla (1996) 7 SCC 668, while noting that those cases involved court sales.

rule.if: completed_property_transaction and purchaser_is_bona_fide and purchaser_created_third_party_interests and no_statutory_bar_applies

predicates.completed_property_transaction: A property transaction has been duly concluded, including transfer of possession or title under the required conveyance.
predicates.purchaser_is_bona_fide: The purchaser acquired the property honestly and without notice of or responsibility for the alleged wrong.
predicates.purchaser_created_third_party_interests: The purchaser or subsequent parties relied on the transaction by creating further property or financial interests.
predicates.no_statutory_bar_applies: No statute requires the purchaser’s interest to be set aside despite the purchaser’s bona fide status.

issues.definition: A bona fide purchaser in a completed transaction is protected from loss when the purchaser created third-party interests and no statute requires a different result.

issues.legal_issue: Delay and laches are relevant to relief in public interest litigation, particularly when parties have changed their positions or third-party interests have arisen, but delay alone does not automatically require dismissal.
material_facts: The challenge was brought after the regulation and clarification had been in operation and after development approvals and transactions had progressed.
Purchasers and developers had acquired rights, undertaken construction or development, and incurred financial liabilities.
The Court found the delay serious but also considered the merits of the challenge.
issues.conclusion: The Court treated delay and laches as an important factor but did not dismiss the petition on that ground alone, having considered the merits.
issues.legal_principle: Equitable principles concerning delay, acquiescence, and third-party interests apply to public interest litigation, but their application depends on the circumstances and the merits. The Court relied on Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000) 10 SCC 664, R. & M. Trust v. Koramangala Residents Vigilance Group (2005) 3 SCC 91, State of Maharashtra v. Digambar (1995) 4 SCC 683, and distinguished M/s. Lohia Machines v. Union of India (AIR 1985 SC 421), where third-party interests had not arisen.

predicates.public_interest_proceeding: The proceeding seeks relief in the public interest.
predicates.substantial_delay: The challenge was brought after a significant period despite the challenged measure or its effects being capable of challenge earlier.
predicates.parties_changed_positions_or_third_party: Parties materially altered their positions or third parties acquired interests before the challenge was determined.

issues.definition: In a public interest proceeding, substantial delay coupled with changed positions or third-party interests matters to relief but does not by itself determine dismissal.
